That is why the “appearances” described in the first part should be called “prehistorical.”
Within History, they are not realized separately, one after another, but all at once.
Historical humanity is therefore always the sum or integration of these appearances, though it is also something more.
Taken together, they form, so to speak, the starting point of the historical process without themselves belonging to that process.
It would actually be more accurate to speak of “pretemporal” elements of human existence, elements which, insofar as they are real, are nevertheless always realized in time.
First, the order in which these elements are described does not correspond to a temporal succession, for the simple reason that they scarcely exist separately in reality.
One therefore cannot genuinely precede another.
Either they all coexist at every moment of time, or they are entirely absent—where human beings do not yet exist.

Second, describing them as pretemporal makes clear that nothing really exists in time that is characterized by desire and sensation alone, or by struggle and perception alone, or by work and reflection alone.

What actually exists are concrete people who desire and sense some particular thing, who struggle for particular goals and perceive particular objects, who work at specific tasks and think about definite problems.
There are no really existing “pure forms” of desire and the rest.
There are only particular things that are desired, sensed, and so on: concrete “contents” that make up the whole existence of the historical human being.
But this concrete, living, historical human being—who realizes definite contents of desire, sensation, and so on in and through his life—will appear only in the second part of the Phenomenology.
We can also say that the elements or foundations of human existence described in the first part are the “conditions of possibility” of that existence.
And because these conditions or premises lie, so to speak, outside human existence or before it, we can say that they do not exist.
The absence of even one of these six moments would make human existence impossible.
There is no human being, and there can be none, without desire, sensation, and the rest.
But neither desire nor sensation exists “by itself,” whether in a human being or in anything else that really exists.

Even taken together, these elements never exist apart from some concrete content determined—or at least capable of being determined—by a historical situation, meaning one of the dialectical stages described in the second part.
Put briefly, the first part describes “abstractions” which, in the form in which they are described, exist only in the phenomenologist’s consciousness.
Desire really exists in every concrete human being, as do the other elements.
But in no one does desire exist in isolation and without a definite content.

Still, because desire, sensation, and the rest really do exist as phenomena within concrete historical human beings, the act of “isolating” and “formalizing” them can itself have a phenomenological character.
So although the “appearances” described in the first part are abstract, they are nevertheless abstract appearances or abstract phenomena.
They are the constituent elements of every real appearance of human beings to human beings.
They have been artificially isolated and stripped of their concrete content.
As such, they never exist within a concrete consciousness.
But no real “appearance” would be possible as an appearance without them.
And insofar as these abstract “appearances” are still appearances—that is, appearances to human beings—their character is not natural but human, and therefore dialectical.
The order in which they are described is therefore not arbitrary.
It is determined by the dialectical relations among them.
But the first part does more than describe these abstract elements or moments of all real human existence—that is, all historical human existence.
It also provides an abstract and formal description of the basic dialectical pattern of that existence.
As we will see, this pattern is defined by three terms:
What was said about the six aspects or moments can also be said of these three basic stages.
They too are “prehistorical” in the sense that every real historical human being is already, in one way or another, a “citizen.”
A real slave or master therefore exists only as a citizen considered under the actual aspect of slavery or mastery.
A slave who exists only as a slave and appears to himself and others only as a slave is just as much an abstraction as “pure” desire.
Every real servile or other form of existence therefore has a concrete content, whereas the first part describes only the pure forms of master, slave, citizen, and so on.
The master, slave, and citizen described in the first part have never existed anywhere in pure form.

But every real form of existence always appears either as that of a “master,” or a “slave,” or a “citizen,” in the sense that it is dominated and determined primarily by the characteristics of the master, slave, or citizen described in the first part.

We can therefore say that the “abstract” slave, master, and citizen of the first part exist nowhere as such, because no actually existing human being ever embodies only one of these fundamental categories.
Furthermore, as we will see, master, slave, and citizen form a dialectical triad: thesis, antithesis, and synthesis.

Once again, although this triad is nowhere realized in time in “pure form”—so that we cannot say, for example, that the master literally exists before the slave—every genuinely historical dialectical process develops according to this pattern.
A stage characterized by the “master” is “negated” in a stage of the “servile” type and is then “dialectically overcome” in a synthetic stage of a “civic” character.

These different formal modes of existence and ways of understanding the world—the master’s, the slave’s, and the citizen’s, as described in the first part—appear again and again throughout humanity’s historical development.
Each time, however, they are filled with new concrete content.

And although we can fully understand what a “master” and so on actually is only from the second part, it would be impossible to identify and understand all the concrete realizations of these forms without first knowing the abstract pattern given in the first part.
This dialectical pattern, because it is the pattern of the dialectical development of phenomena, is itself dialectical in character.
That is why even the first part of the Phenomenology can be called phenomenology: it concerns the “appearances” of nature and humanity to human beings.
But it is almost impossible to speak about these phenomenological abstractions without at the same time speaking about their cosmological and sometimes ontological counterparts.
The danger of confusing the phenomenological “level” with the cosmological and ontological levels is therefore especially great in this first part of the Phenomenology.
The second part—the properly phenomenological part—will describe the phenomenological side of humanity’s historical existence, so to speak, “from Antiquity to the present.”

Here the phenomenologist is no longer dealing with abstractions but with the most concrete human reality possible: historical actuality—or, more exactly, the history of each way in which the natural and human world “appears” to human beings.

Because of this, we can say that the order of the description generally follows the chronological order in which the “appearances” themselves emerged. But the two do not coincide completely, for a reason we have already mentioned: the “thesis” often takes its final form only after the “antithesis” has already appeared. In other words, the thesis being described may actually be later in time than the antithesis being described, and so on. Broadly speaking, everything we have already said about the Phenomenology as a whole applies to this second part, because this second part is precisely the Phenomenology in the strict sense of the word. We still have to discuss some of its particular structural features.
But first we need to say a few words about the third and final part of the Phenomenology, entitled “The Post-Historical Existence of Human Beings.”

This part will deal with communism—that is, with the future. And insofar as it remains phenomenological, it will deal with the way this future appears to the human being of the present: namely, to the socialist.

We know, however, that the historical future is “negative,” or free, and therefore unpredictable. This third part will consequently have a “hypothetical” character. The future it describes as an “appearance” may never become present reality—that is, may never become “authentic”—and may remain forever only a “project” for humanity. The most the Phenomenology can do here is show that this project is not “utopian”: that it has real roots in an already existing historical reality, or more precisely in the way that reality appears to the actually existing human being of the present.

The Phenomenology can also show that communism will appear as an antithesis to the entire historical process described in the second part, and that it will therefore be a non-historical “appearance” of nature and humanity to human beings. But the phenomenologist can hardly go beyond this purely negative definition. He cannot say anything positive about future “communist” phenomena.

So if this entire third part belongs to the Phenomenology in the strict sense, it does so only in order to show that the Phenomenology is not final. In other words, the socialist end of History does not yet mean, strictly speaking, either the end of human existence as such or the completion of the dialectic itself. And since all the phenomena known to us have a historical—that is, sociopolitical or collective—character, we can say nothing positive about communist phenomena, which will necessarily have an individual character.

We can therefore know that, if a final “communist” Phenomenology is ever written, it will contain two main sections. The first will contain our socialist or historical Phenomenology—though obviously without its third part. The second will replace that third part with a complete description of all the “appearances” of the communist world.
But we cannot know what that section will contain. That is the “secret of the future.”

We still have to discuss some of the structural features of the Phenomenology, especially those of its second and central part. First, we need to look at the characteristic phenomenological omissions and repetitions. Then we will consider the way the exposition divides into two parallel sections, one describing the “real” and the other the “ideal” aspects of historical “appearances.”

We have already had occasion to discuss the omissions and shortcuts that are so striking in the Phenomenology. Its second part will describe the phenomenological aspect of the dialectical development of humanity as a whole—in short, universal history “from Antiquity to the present day.” Obviously, a relatively short book must leave out the overwhelming majority of historical facts. In this respect, the Phenomenology is no different from a good old-fashioned history course. Like the historian, the phenomenologist discusses only what seems especially important and decisive in the process of historical development and, in some sense, in the overall picture he forms of that development.

Even so, the Phenomenology will seem much more fragmentary to the reader than an ordinary historical account of roughly the same length. More importantly, the phenomenologist selects his historical material in a fundamentally different way from the ordinary historian.

The reason is that the historian and the phenomenologist have different aims—or, if you prefer, different subjects and objects of study. I mean here the non-Marxist historian: the “scholar” who is not also a philosopher.

On the one hand, because the phenomenologist is a philosopher, he deals with concrete historical reality and therefore understands it as dialectical. On the other hand, because he is a phenomenologist, he is interested exclusively in the phenomenological side of that dialectic.

The Phenomenology therefore does not describe the chronological sequence of historical “events” in general. It describes the dialectical sequence of theses, antitheses, and syntheses, selecting only those that seem essential to the movement of dialectical development.

And however long a thesis, antithesis, or synthesis lasts, however many “historical events” it contains, the phenomenologist treats each of them as a single whole, a single “appearance,” and describes its characteristic features as a whole.

This is why the chronological “jumps” in the Phenomenology are usually much larger than the corresponding gaps in a scholarly history. But the Phenomenology does not describe each thesis, antithesis, or synthesis as it really is—that is, as Cosmology or Marxist History would describe it. It describes it only as an appearance or phenomenon.

In other words, it does not describe the real structure that constitutes the thesis, antithesis, and so on of a particular historical period. It describes the way that period “appears” to the corresponding “consciousness”: the way it is “reflected” in the self-consciousness of the people who live through it.

Naturally, the phenomenologist will choose the fullest and clearest possible “reflection” of a given period. But complete understanding of an age does not necessarily arise at the moment when that age first appears. It may emerge only after the age itself has definitively “died.” As a result, the phenomenologist’s selection can be extremely uneven in chronological terms. Sometimes only a few years separate the “appearances” he describes; sometimes whole centuries or even millennia lie between them.

The phenomenologist therefore seems to “jump” from thesis to antithesis, and then onward again, without describing—as the historian does—the continuous and unbroken chain of events that actually connects the phenomena in question.

Indeed, strictly speaking, he does not describe historical “events” at all. What he describes are not events in the proper sense, but only their “reflections”—or, more precisely, the reflections of all the events that together make up a particular dialectical stage.
Reading the Phenomenology therefore assumes that the reader already knows the general course of real History and the main “historical events” that compose it.

But the “reflections” of events in consciousness also have a “history” of their own, and anyone reading the Phenomenology will find it useful to know at least its broad outlines. For, as I have already said, here too the phenomenologist jumps from one complete and vivid—or, as we say, “adequate”—reflection to another, without describing the historical process through which one reflection developed into the next.
To give a preliminary idea of what the Phenomenology “contains,” and of what it selects and describes, I will quote a few pages from the “Preface” to Hegel’s Phenomenology.

It is not difficult to see, Hegel writes (p. 15 ff.), that our time is a time in which a new age is being born. Humanity has broken with the old world in which it has until now existed and imagined itself. It is preparing to consign that world to the past and is transforming it through work.

Human beings, of course, are never at rest but are always moving forward. Yet just as an infant, after a long period of silent nourishment in the womb, suddenly interrupts the gradual and merely quantitative process of growth with its first breath—a qualitative leap that marks its birth—so humanity, as it forms itself, slowly and silently matures toward a new shape [Gestalt].

One by one, it loosens the pieces of the structure that made up its previous world, so that at first only isolated symptoms reveal that the old world has begun to totter. The frivolity and boredom that spread through what still survives, together with the vague anticipation of something unknown, are the first signs that something different is coming.

This gradual disintegration, which does not yet alter the overall appearance of the whole, is suddenly interrupted by sunrise. Like a flash of lightning, it reveals at once the appearance [Gebild] of a new world.

But this new world is no more fully real at first than a child is fully developed at birth. It is essential not to lose sight of this. Its first appearance is only its immediacy, or its abstract and schematic concept.

Just as a building is not finished when only its foundations have been laid, the concept of the whole that has now been reached is not yet the whole itself. If we want to see an oak in the full strength of its trunk, the spread of its branches, and the mass of its leaves, we are not satisfied if we are shown an acorn instead.
The same is true of science—that is, the complete and concrete understanding of a human world. Science is not finished at the moment that world begins.

The beginning of the new human being is the product of a long revolutionary transformation [Umwälzung] of many different cultural forms, the result of a winding path repeatedly travelled and of repeated struggle and effort.
This beginning is the whole that has returned into itself from both its succession and its extension. It is the simple, that is, abstract, concept of the whole that has come into being [gewordene].

The real actuality of this simple whole consists in the fact that the old forms [Gestaltungen], which have now become superseded moments or elements of a new whole, develop and take shape once again—but now within their new medium [Elemente] and within the meaning that has itself come into being.
